title: The SCIP Optimization Suite 5.0
contribution: Release report of the SCIP Optimization Suite 5.0 (22 authors, Gleixner first): it documents the components behind a 1.41x (MIP) and 1.17x (MINLP) speed-up over SCIP 4, measured with five seeds and time brackets on 417 MIP and 105 MINLP instances that some tested version solves, and adds SoPlex 3.1, SCIP-SDP warmstarts, SCIP-Jack 1.2 and UG 0.8.5; the report credits Gleixner as co-implementer of the OBBT-based bilinear strengthening, nonzero cancellation, the linear-constraint classification and the activation of SoPlex polishing.
problem_entry: Enters through the release (new features, speed over SCIP 4 when used out of the box) and poses the measurement problem first: performance variability needs a careful methodology, and the 87 MIPLIB 2010 benchmark instances are too few for robust results (pp. 3, 6). Each component starts from a named shortfall of SCIP 4: cut routines that cannot reuse a base inequality, root-only cuts, no symmetry handling, bound-exceeding LP analysis off, expensive LNS heuristics switched off, McCormick missing the hull under extra linear constraints (pp. 5, 13, 18-21, 24).
key_idea: Many components, each measured: cut scoring by efficacy, objective parallelism and integral support with a parallelism filter (0.1, or 0.5 for cuts within 0.9 of the best) and cuts at local nodes via the pool (pp. 17-18); an aggregation API with double-double arithmetic (p. 18); CMIR plus lifted flow cover from one base inequality (p. 19); dual solution analysis (p. 21); bandit-coordinated ALNS (pp. 23-24); orbital fixing or symretopes (pp. 13-16); polishing in probing and diving (p. 28). In AG's own component, auxiliary LPs over the relaxation yield, through their duals, up to four two-variable inequalities per bilinear term, which Locatelli's convex-hull formulas then use (p. 20).
assumptions: MIP (1); MINLP (2) with nonconvex f, g given in algebraic form with operators known to SCIP; CIP: an LP or NLP remains once the integers are fixed (pp. 4-5). Symmetry for binaries only, over the formulation group, with every other symmetry-breaking component switched off or SCIP may call a non-optimal solution optimal (pp. 13, 16). Nonzero cancellation only with W = empty set, structure-preserving and |lambda| <= 1000 (p. 11); disaggregation only for block-separable quadratics (p. 12); bilinear strengthening only for terms in nonconvex quadratic constraints (p. 20); CMIR gains depend on fixed-charge network structure (p. 19). Libraries: COR@L, MIPLIB up to 2010, MINLPLib2, CBLIB, UFCN, ULSB, Margot's 16 (pp. 6, 16, 19, 34).
proof_devices: Clique table: Tarjan SCCs on the implication graph aggregate equal literals; a path u -> not-u fixes u = 0; a second run from the last node of the topological order; cliques entered at most twice, arcs implicit (p. 10)
Nonzero cancellation: nonzero change |U| - |W| > 0; candidate pairs by hashing variable-pair coefficient quadruples instead of a quadratic search; |lambda| <= 1000 numerical guard (pp. 10-11)
Disaggregation (5)-(6) equivalent to (4); without it up to the product of m_p inequalities; partition size capped at 127; scaled so reformulated-feasible implies original-feasible (p. 12)

Symmetry: FD inequalities rejected for exponential coefficients; minimal-cover (Balas-Jeroslow) ternary formulations of symresacks separable in O(n alpha(n)); orbisack facets in linear time; full orbitopes via n-1 orbisacks with O(mn) separation and recursive O(mn) propagation (pp. 13-15)
Orbital fixing (Lemma 2.1) on the subgroup generated by the generators that keep B1 invariant, valid because Sigma(i) is contained in Stab(B1)(i) (pp. 15-16)

Cut management: efficacy = Euclidean distance, parallelism = cosine; greedy selection with a parallelism filter; cut-pool threshold eta adapted after Andreello et al.; post-processing by maximal dynamism, scaling, coefficient strengthening (pp. 17-18)
CMIR: rows scored by fractionality influence; efficacies of k scaling factors in O(k*n + m) by aggregating the continuous part (p. 19)
Bilinear strengthening: LP (9) from corner s towards corner t over the relaxation; the optimal duals give inequality (10); run inside prop_obbt under its iteration limit (p. 20)
Dual solution analysis: the dual (12) of a bound-exceeding LP gives inequality (13), globally valid and violated on the local box; dual-ray analysis is the special case c = 0, z* = 0 (p. 21)
Double-double arithmetic (Rump): unevaluated sum of two doubles, branch-free, exact sum of two doubles in 6 additions, used in cut separation (p. 25)
Numerical violation report: maximum absolute and relative violations, a lower bound unless every handler implements the update (p. 26)

SDP rounding problems: optval(P-R) <= optval(SDP-P) <= optval(SDP-D) <= optval(D-R), so equality certifies the SDP optimum by LPs and (P-R) can prune nodes; eigenvalue clipping P_lambda (14) (pp. 32-33)
experiments: SCIP 5.0.0+SoPlex 3.1.0 vs SCIP 4.0.0+SoPlex 3.0.0 on 417 MIP (from 666, 19 infeasible) and 105 MINLP instances selected by a stated solvability funnel; five seeds (random for MIP, permutation for MINLP because it varies more), (instance, seed) pairs as observations, shifted geometric means with shifts 1 s and 100 nodes, 0.5 s floor, brackets plus diff-timeouts and per-library rows, 7200 s with zero gap (MIP) and 3600 s with gap 1e-4 (MINLP), one job per machine (pp. 6-8). MIP 1.41 (2.07 on [100,7200]), timeouts 403 -> 217; MINLP 1.17, timeouts 125 -> 105 (pp. 8-9). Component numbers dated to their merge, mostly with seed zero, flagged as not reproducible in the strict sense (pp. 9-28); SDP warmstarts on 320 instances (p. 34); UG-MISDP on one instance (p. 36). Failures reported (pp. 19, 24, 34-35). 16 MIP and 10 MINLP observations dropped as errors, not itemized (inferred). No significance test.
positioning: Against its own predecessor only: every run compares SCIP 5 with SCIP 4 or toggles a component; no other MIP or MINLP solver is run (pp. 8-36). Methodology credited to Achterberg-Wunderling (brackets) and Danna, Lodi-Tramontani (variability) (pp. 6-8); techniques adopted with explicit credit (Wesselmann-Suhl, Andreello et al., Achterberg et al. [5], Hojny-Pfetsch, Kaibel-Pfetsch, Margot, Locatelli, Rothberg, Rump; pp. 11-25); claims over other solvers only for SCIP-Jack, by reference (p. 30); his own OBBT [42], iterative refinement [43] and Vigerske-Gleixner [100] serve as infrastructure (pp. 4, 12, 20).
writing: The abstract gives two numbers per problem class, each tied to a subset, and the headline always uses the 'all' row (smaller factor for MIP, larger for MINLP) (pp. 3, 8-9). Bullets follow each table with a note on reading the metrics (p. 8). Hedges sit next to their number (pp. 8, 9, 20), and 'At the time of ...' dates each component number (pp. 10, 11, 18, 28). Adjectives appear beside counts (pp. 8, 19, 30), one bullet smooths its table (p. 9), negatives are stated plainly (pp. 34-35), and a contribution map closes the report (pp. 37-38).
limits_future: MINLP sets smaller and less diverse (p. 9); component numbers from intermediate versions, mostly one seed (p. 9); symmetry for binaries only (p. 13); bilinear effect not yet evaluated (p. 20); MPEC no major effect (pp. 22-23); further multi-NLP-solver uses not implemented (p. 27); SDP warmstarts off by default, with two remedies named for the rounding problems (p. 35); UG-MISDP analysis pending (p. 36). Future: bandit selection for other components (pp. 24-25), classical SPG for SCIP-Jack (p. 30), better MINLP benchmark sets (p. 9).

method_links.note: The development test set is an instrument built by written rules with counts (666 -> 417 MIP with 19 infeasible; 143 -> 105 MINLP), MIPLIB-2010 'numerically unstable' instances removed, and the filter's bias direction argued. Its limits are printed: MIPLIB 2010 benchmark too small, MINLP sets less diverse. Cross-check (S002 file pp. 13, 17 only): MIPLIB 2017 presolved with SCIP 5.0 for its features, and its 'Constraint classification' feature group has the same 17 linear-constraint types that SCIP 5.0 ships (pp. 26-27), built by Hendel 'together with AG' (p. 37).

Release form: default against default (SCIP 5.0.0+SoPlex 3.1.0 vs SCIP 4.0.0+SoPlex 3.0.0), every third-party version listed and the mismatch named (SoPlex version, no bliss in SCIP 4); the co-released LP solver counts as part of the treatment and no reduced baseline is built. Like-for-like comparisons switch one component in one build (orbital fixing vs no symmetry handling). Table 3 changes the baseline to SCIP 4.0.1+SoPlex 3.0.1 without comment. The latest bugfix release as a second baseline (step 10) comes later.

Gaps printed where they arise, with size or cause: symmetry for binaries only; bilinear evaluation 'still to be conducted' (AG's own component); multi-NLP-solver uses not implemented; SDP rounding problems cut off over 25% / 50% of relaxations but cost too much, with two named remedies (a lost experiment read as the next step); UG-MISDP analysis pending; bandit selection for other components, API already public. Mostly group work.

Floating-point release: precision is raised only where round-off threatens validity. Cut aggregation and generation use double-double, and GMP is ruled out as 'orders of magnitudes slower'; the accuracy gained is spent on deleting numerics-motivated cut rejection rules (rank limit, small integral scaling). Dangerous constructions are avoided by design: FD inequalities with exponential coefficients, |lambda| > 1000 in nonzero cancellation (AG co-implementer), unscaled disaggregated quadratics. A cheap mid-precision step ahead of the later safe cuts, not exact arithmetic deciding.

Correctness is screened, not certified: runs with bounds inconsistent with a known optimal value are dropped from 'all'; accepted solutions report maximum violations as a lower bound; the symmetry section names the component interaction that would make SCIP call a non-optimal solution optimal. No independent checker or exact verification in this release.

The solver carries instruments 'to trigger performance variability systematically' (centralized random seed from SCIP 4, permutation seed), but one belief stays unmeasured and is labelled as such: the MINLP gap limit 1e-4 rests on a 'repeated observation' about variability near small gaps that the authors say they have not quantified systematically.

Each default rests on a measurement dated to its merge (clique table analysis, {0,1/2}-cuts, bound-exceeding LP analysis switched on in 5.0, ALNS, polishing in probing and diving with AG); components stay off or restricted where they do not pay (SCIP-SDP warmstarts off, MPEC conservative limits, aggressive scaling by flag, polishing out of strong branching and OBBT).

Each component gets its metric: primal integral and time to first solution (structure heuristics), calls/improving/optimal finds 42/6/2 (MPEC), root gap (bilinear), SDP iterations with penalty and unsolved shares (warmstarts), nodes with time (dual solution analysis); null results said plainly.

Five seeds with each (instance, seed) pair one observation in 2017, before the three-seed sentence of 2021; brackets with a reason for each exclusion, a diff-timeouts row, per-library subsets; shifts, 0.5 s floor, unsolved runs charged the time limit; the collection filter's bias argued; a shorter time limit 'slightly favors the weaker solver'.

Exclusions for errors and bound inconsistencies are neither counted nor named: by my arithmetic, 417x5 = 2085 vs 2069 MIP and 105x5 = 525 vs 515 MINLP observations, so 16 and 10 were dropped (inferred from the tables).

Use what the solver has already computed: AG's bilinear strengthening reads inequalities off the duals of auxiliary LPs solved inside the existing OBBT propagator under its iteration budget; Witzig's dual solution analysis turns a bound-exceeding LP's dual into a globally valid propagation constraint.
Halving the timeouts (403 -> 217) is called the most important result; newly solved instances are featured (macrophage, ULSB mostly at the root, formerly unsolved MWCSP).

Byline detail: the December 2017 report lists Gleixner first and the other 21 alphabetically, like the SCIP 4.0 report with Maher first, so 'alphabetical' release bylines mean the lead first and the rest alphabetical.
Significance testing: none in this report; variability is hedged by seeds and brackets.

SCIP 5.0 lead (first author); his own code in the release is the MINLP and presolve components, the classification tool and an LP-solver integration; exact rational solving appears only as SoPlex's feature via [43].

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: two-tier evidence in a release report
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The headline comes from a strict protocol (final versions, five seeds, exclusive machines); component numbers are dated to their merge ('At the time of ...') and covered by one caveat saying they may not reproduce with the release. Close to the MIPLIB 2017 rule that non-exclusive runs must not be confused with a benchmark (SKILL.md, M17 p. 480).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: the release ships the measurement instruments
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SCIP 5.0 adds numerical-violation queries, statistics-table plugins, the linear-constraint classification (Hendel with AG) and a bandit API, on top of SCIP 4's seeds; tests run on Ipet and Rubberband (github.com/ambros-gleixner/rubberband). The same 17-type classification reappears as MIPLIB 2017's feature group (S002 file p. 17; whether its extractor calls SCIP's code is not stated there).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: contribution map in a multi-author software report
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A closing section maps every section to its implementers and 'possible contact points'; it is also what separates Gleixner's 2017 code from group work.

transferable: Build a development test set as a funnel with a count at each step (public pool; minus flagged-unstable and duplicate instances; old and new versions run on five seeds, non-exclusively, at a slightly raised time limit; keep what at least one version solves on at least one seed), then state which way the filter biases the comparison (p. 6).

Report brackets [s, T] defined by the slower version and requiring at least one solve, plus a diff-timeouts row, with each (instance, seed) pair as one observation; floor times at 0.5 s, use shifts of 1 s and 100 nodes, and charge unsolved runs the time limit while counting them separately (pp. 7-8).
Choose the perturbation per problem class by which one produces more variability (random seed for MIP, permutation seed for MINLP) (p. 7).

Date each component measurement to its merge and put one reproducibility caveat before the component sections; footnote the direction of a time-limit bias (a shorter limit favours the weaker solver) (pp. 9, 16).
For a reduction that relies on an invariant (symmetry), list the components that must be switched off and the wrong answer that follows otherwise (p. 16).
Run aggregation-heavy cut generation in double-double (branch-free, 6 additions for an exact sum), then delete rejection rules that existed only because of round-off (pp. 18, 25).
After a reformulation, scale the new constraints so that feasibility within tolerance for them implies feasibility for the original constraint (p. 12).
Report maximum absolute and relative violations of every accepted solution, called a lower bound when not every handler computes them (p. 26).

Generate missing side constraints for a convex-hull formula with small auxiliary LPs inside an existing propagator, reading each inequality off the LP duals and sharing the propagator's iteration budget (p. 20).
Rate a primal heuristic by calls, improving finds and optimal finds (42/6/2) and by primal integral and time to first solution, not only by solving time (pp. 22-23).
In a multi-author software paper, add a section that names the implementers of each feature (pp. 37-38).
coauthors: L. Eifler, T. Gally, G. Gamrath, P. Gemander, R. L. Gottwald, G. Hendel, C. Hojny, T. Koch, M. Miltenberger, B. Müller, M. E. Pfetsch, C. Puchert, D. Rehfeldt, F. Schlösser, F. Serrano, Y. Shinano, J. M. Viernickel, S. Vigerske, D. Weninger, J. T. Witt, J. Witzig (Gleixner first, the rest alphabetical; p. 3). AG's code per p. 37: nonzero cancellation (with Gemander, Gottwald, Weninger), bilinear relaxations (with Müller, Serrano), linear-constraint classification (with Hendel), SoPlex polishing inside SCIP (with Miltenberger).

quotes.text: Thus, the performance results reported below provide a conservatively biased evaluation, that is, possibly, a slight underestimation of the improvements achieved by SCIP 5 for instances that can be solved to optimality.
Hence, not all of the results reported in the following may be reproducible in the most strict sense using the final release version of SCIP 5.
